findings.title: integerToBytes returns wrong array in left-padding branch
findings.body: In the `qLength > bytes.length` branch of `integerToBytes`, the method allocates a left-padded `tmp` array of `qLength` bytes and copies `bytes` into it, but then returns `bytes` (the original shorter array) instead of `tmp`. The left-padding is therefore never applied. This causes `asn1derToConcatenatedRS` to call `System.arraycopy(r, 0, concatenatedSignatureValue, 0, len)` with `r.length < len`, which throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` whenever the BigInteger R or S value happens to be shorter than `qLength` (e.g. when the high byte of the value is 0, which is statistically possible for ECDSA signatures). The fix is to return `tmp` on line 160.

findings.title: Dead code in concatenatedRSToASN1DER discards encoder results
findings.body: The two statements `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` create encoders, write to them, and immediately discard the results. The actual encoding used for the return value is produced by the subsequent `writeDerSeq(...)` call. The dead code is confusing and wasteful, and should be removed.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider does not return a BouncyCastle provider
findings.body: `AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which is the provider backing the default JCA keystore (typically SunJCE on a standard JDK, or the BC provider only if it has been registered globally). The method is named `getBouncyCastleProvider` and the interface contract in `CryptoProvider` documents it as returning the BouncyCastle security provider, so any caller that relies on this method to obtain BouncyCastle (e.g. to invoke BC-specific APIs) will silently get the wrong provider. Since the authz-client is intended to avoid the BouncyCastle dependency, the method should return `null` or the implementation should be renamed/document so the contract is not violated.

findings.title: Indefinite-length encoding returned as -1 but not handled by callers
findings.body: `readLength()` returns `-1` for indefinite-length encoding (length byte 0x80). Callers like `readSequence()` then evaluate `while (length > 0)`, which immediately exits and returns an empty list, while `readInteger()` would pass `-1` to `read(int)`, which throws an `IOException` with a misleading 'EOF found reading -1 bytes' message. Indefinite-length encoding is not legal in DER and should be rejected explicitly (e.g. throw an `IOException` for `0x80`) instead of being silently passed through.

findings.title: Test does not cover the case where R/S is shorter than the curve length
findings.body: The test only exercises the round-trip with default JDK-generated EC keys and a fixed message. For typical ES256 signatures the BigInteger byte arrays of R and S are 32 or 33 bytes long, so the `qLength > bytes.length` branch of `integerToBytes` is never entered and the `return bytes` bug on line 160 of `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` is not detected. A test that explicitly constructs DER signatures where R or S is shorter than `algorithm.getSignatureLength() / 2` (e.g. by zero-padding the high byte) would trigger the `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` described above. Without such a test the bug will not be caught by CI.

findings.title: Adding order() to CryptoProvider is a binary-incompatible API change
findings.body: A new abstract method `int order()` has been added to the `org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider` interface. This is part of the public `keycloak-common` artifact: any out-of-tree implementation of `CryptoProvider` (extensions, integrators, third-party crypto providers) will fail to compile/link against the new interface. This should be called out in the release notes / migration guide so downstream users know they must add an `order()` method to their implementation. Additionally, consider providing a `default` implementation (e.g. `return 0;`) to make the change source-compatible for the common case.
